chunks: Analog versus digital signals. The question: What is the difference between analog and digital?
An analog signal can take any value in a range, and its exact value carries the message.
A digital signal only has a few allowed levels, usually two, and the message is which level it is at. Digital buys immunity to noise and perfect copying.
The price is lost fine detail and extra conversion hardware.
Think of a ramp versus a staircase. A ball on a ramp can rest at any height, so if someone nudges it, it stays at the new height and the error is permanent.
A ball on a staircase rests on a step, so a small nudge still leaves it on the same step. That is why digital resists noise.
The picture hides one thing: a real signal switching from low to high passes through the in-between voltages on the way.
The waveform is distorted by about ±0.
37 volts of noise, but it never enters the band between V IL and V IH once settled, so a receiver reads exactly the same bits as if there was no noise.
Analog information would be corrupted.
Analog signal: a signal whose exact value, at any moment, carries the information. Digital signal: a signal read as one of a few allowed levels, such as 0 or 1.
Threshold: the voltage at which a receiver decides between low and high. Noise margin: how much unwanted noise a logic level can absorb before it is misread.
Quantization: rounding an analog value to the nearest of a fixed set of levels, as an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) does.
Take 3. 3 volts logic. A receiver reads anything above 2. 0 volts as high and anything below 0. 8 volts as low. A driver promises at least 2. 4 volts for high and at most 0.
4 volts for low. That leaves 0. 4 volts of margin on each side, so 0. 3 volts of noise changes nothing, and the next logic chip restores a clean level.
Now convert an analog voltage with a 12-bit ADC and a 3. 3 volts range. It has 4096 levels, each 0. 806 millivolts wide. Anything finer is lost. That is the whole idea.
"Analog signals are continuous in value and time, so the exact voltage carries the information.
Digital signals are limited to a few levels, usually two, so the information is just which side of a threshold you're on.
That gives you noise immunity, exact copying and easy processing, at the cost of needing ADCs and DACs and some bandwidth.
And remember a digital wire is still an analog waveform: edges, ringing and noise margins still matter."
